The Singer Growth Economy Top 50
It is a pleasure to support the 
publication of The Singer Growth 
Economy Top 50 and to see such 
an exciting array of UK businesses 
shaping the future. 
The crises and shocks of the last 
few years have left our country 
facing an unprecedented set of 
challenges. The Government must 
now solve a seemingly impossible 
equation as recession looms, 
inflation soars and monetary policy 
tightens. 
While there is much disagreement 
around the policy choices of today, 
there is one thing everyone can 
agree on: productivity and growth 
must be achieved in the future 
if we are to restore the health of 
our economy. It is therefore more 
important than ever that the capital 
markets’ ecosystem supports 
entrepreneurs, growth companies 
and their investors. 
Our list of the top 50 companies 
spans across a wide variety of 
sectors—from mobile apps and AI 
technology, to innovative healthcare 
solutions and nutrition. With an 
impressive mean turnover of £39.1m 
(based on those filing full accounts) 
and a mean employee count of 197, 
these business champions look 
set to dominate in their respective 
fields over the coming months and 
years to come. 
Of particular note is the sector-
wide development in AI and 
machine learning technology as this 
becomes more and more integrated 
into our daily lives. Companies such 
as Quantexa, a Yorkshire-based 
business that develops technology 
using AI and big data software to 
flag illegal activity within a user’s 
network, are leading the way in 
business resilience and cyber 
security. On the other end of the 
spectrum, we have Wayve—a 
London-based tech business who 
are challenging conventional 
transport with the development of 
software for self-driving cars that 
use machine learning technology. 
The global paradigm shift in 
energy consumption is becoming 
more prevalent than ever as the 
UK and the rest of the world set 
ambitious Net Zero targets. At the 
heart of this, it’s fantastic to see 
UK businesses leading the way 
in the solutions our country so 
desperately needs. 
The app economy is also thriving 
as we see a large handful of 
businesses featured in the top 50. 
Challenger banks Monzo, Monese, 
Moneybox and Revolut all feature 
as alternative banking solutions 
whilst mobile apps Pedal Me and 
Thrive provide convenient health 
and wellbeing solutions. 
As we look to the future and what 
this might hold, Singer Capital 
Markets is delighted to operate 
at the heart of this ecosystem, 
providing access to capital, 
advice and liquidity. This autumn 
we launched The Singer Growth 
Economy initiative to highlight the 
key growth drivers of tomorrow’s 
economy and the innovators, 
disruptors and challengers that 
we believe will be the winners. 
Through this framework, we 
highlight opportunities across 
four overarching themes: Health 
and Wellbeing of the Population, 
Transition to a Sustainable 
Economy, Innovation and Emerging 
Technologies, and Geopolitics and 
Demographics. More information 
about The Singer Growth Economy 
can be found on page 3. 
While the UK economy faces a 
difficult time ahead, this report 
highlights 50 companies and 10 
rising stars that are set to buck the 
trend. The Singer Growth Economy 
investment landscape enjoyed a 
particularly healthy period in 2021 
with £24.9b equity investment 
secured. Despite headwinds, 
growth companies were still able to 
secure a record equity investment 
in the first half of 2022, proving the 
resilience and confidence in these 
exciting UK businesses.

Introducing the 
Singer Growth Economy
Genomic-based technologies, personalised and 
preventative, biology-led discovery, efficiency 
through the cycle from discovery to consumer, health 
monitoring, nutrition. 
 
In recent years, healthcare systems and the life 
sciences industry have undergone tremendous 
changes given technological, regulatory and 
socioeconomic disruptions. The net outcome of these 
changes is the continued convergence of healthcare, 
technology and retail and consumer industries such 
that in the next decade healthcare will be centred 
on human needs, and will be personalised, digitised 
and preventative, with healthcare solutions being 
seamlessly integrated into daily life.
Security of supply chains and re-industrialisation 
of the developed world, national security and 
defence, developing working practices and 
attitudes, increasing and more complex regulation, 
democratisation of finance and emerging global 
wealth, consumer evolution, education. 
 
The combination of policy and technology can tackle 
some of most pressing geopolitical and demographic 
challenges. By improving the security of supply chains, 
re-industrialising developed economies, and helping 
companies and individuals to innovate in complex 
regulatory environments, we can give everyone a 
chance to prosper. Similarly, by using technology to 
support access to finance and encourage greater 
consumer rights, we can help to create a more stable 
and just world.
Climate change and energy transition, water, 
energy and food security, advanced materials, 
21st century infrastructure, waste management, 
recycling and product life, growing and aging 
population. 
 
The sustainable economy is an alternative vision for 
growth and development built on transformational 
technological drivers that are required to address 
climate and environmental challenges. It involves 
using building materials and energy efficiencies to 
deliver circular economy solutions that will result in 
fewer negative impacts on the natural environment 
and that will better support social wellbeing.
Digitisation and process automation, business 
resilience and cyber security, data infrastructure 
and analytics, cloud computing, blockchain 
technology, communications infrastructure, 
creative entertainment. 
 
Human progress is driven by the power of ideas 
and their translation into new technologies. By 
overcoming challenges using technology, humans 
have created greater prosperity for ourselves and 
for future generations. Change is accelerating 
and new technologies are helping to digitise 
and automate processes, make businesses more 
resilient to cyber security threats, improve data 
infrastructure and analytics, and to make it easier to 
communicate and share the most important stories.

In these uncertain times, it is 
more important than ever for us 
to nurture and support growth 
companies. Our economy must 
recoup the considerable costs of 
recent crises, and our firm belief is 
that this can only be achieved by 
stimulating productivity in our great 
nation’s innovators, disrupters, and 
challengers. 
 
The Singer Growth Economy 
highlights opportunities across 
four overarching themes: health 
and wellbeing of the population, 
transition to a sustainable 
economy, innovation and emerging 
technologies, and geopolitics and 
demographics. Within these themes, 
we have identified what we believe to 
be the most powerful growth drivers 
shaping the future of our economy, 
playing out not over months or even 
years, but over decades. 
 
To learn more about The Singer 
Growth Economy and to explore 
other related content, visit the Singer 
Capital Markets website.

The Singer Growth Economy Top 50
 
 
 
The Singer Growth Economy report 
shines a light on an incredible and 
diverse group of growing companies—
all the more important in turbulent 
times. From ZOE which uses machine 
learning to provide users with 
personalised dietary recommendations 
to online games developer Build A 
Rocket Boy, the more than 40,000 
companies (including the Top 50) that 
make up the Singer Growth Economy are 
high-growth and innovating in different 
sectors and regions across the UK. 
 
When we talk about private companies 
as an asset class—and generating 
investment statistics—we treat 
companies as a homogenous group. 
While this provides a sensible high-level 
view of investment volumes, it is in some 
regards a way of comparing apples with 
oranges. A growth-stage SaaS platform 
and a seed-stage battery technology 
spinout are fundamentally different. 
 
Part of the beauty of the Singer Growth 
Economy is that it focuses an analytical 
lens on companies that are innovating 
in four key thematic areas that will 
change the future of the UK economy: 
health and wellbeing of the population; 
transition to a sustainable economy; 
innovation and emerging technologies; 
and geopolitics and demographics. 
 
Future and growth-focused companies 
are investable regardless of the 
economic environment. Good ideas 
with a strong team behind them can 
win out despite headwinds. The Top 
50 companies presented here are not 
only growing headcount or turnover at 
a phenomenal rate, these companies 
have also grown their valuations by at 
least 15% during the last three years. 
 
While the macroeconomic environment 
has changed, these companies have 
the trajectory that may make many 
of them household names in the 
years to come; some already are. 
The UK economy needs more growth 
champions—perhaps now more than 
ever. We look forward to seeing the 
Singer Growth Economy companies 
ascend to new heights.
Henry Whorwood,

Methodological overview
This report analyses the 40.6k private, high-growth companies that 
comprise the Singer Growth Economy. Companies that met one of 
Beauhurst’s eight triggers (see opposite) and that have operations in 
at least one of the Singer Growth Economy Themes (page 3) are in 
scope. 
 
The report also includes a ranking of the Top 50 high-growth 
companies using a three-year compound annual growth rate (CAGR) 
for the higher of turnover or employee headcount. To be eligible for 
the ranking, companies need to have grown their valuation by at 
least a 15% CAGR between 01/07/2019 and 30/06/2022 based on at 
least two equity finance deals during the period. 
 
Filings at Companies House have been used to determine the pre-
money and post-money valuations of the companies at the time of 
the equity finance deal. More detailed methodological information is 
available in the methodological notes in the appendix.
Beauhurst identifies ambitious businesses using eight triggers (outlined 
at the bottom of this page) that we believe suggests a company has 
high-growth potential. More detail on Beauhurst’s tracking triggers is 
available via our website.  
 
Equity investment 
To be included in our analysis, any investment must be:
• 
Some form of equity investment
• 
Secured by a non-listed UK company
• 
Issued between 1 January 2012 and 31 December 2021
 
Announced and unannounced fundraisings 
An unannounced fundraising is an investment made into a private 
company that is completed without press coverage or a statement 
from the recipient company or funds that made the investment. These 
transactions are an integral part of the UK’s high-growth economy, 
accounting for around 70% of all equity transactions.

Population health refers to the general 
health and wellbeing of the whole 
population. Factors affecting access 
to a healthy lifestyle include socio-
economic and environmental disparities, 
alongside individual lifestyle factors. 
In 2020, the UK population was over 
67m with an average life expectancy 
of 80.4 years. The Office for National 
Statistics suggests the population will 
increase by 3.2% in the next decade to 
69.2m. As the population increases and 
ages, discrepancies in health between 
the poorest and richest regions may 
continue. In regions where there is 
higher educational attainment, higher 
average salaries, and fewer economic 
inequalities people generally live a 
higher quality of life. 
 
Technology will play a key role in closing 
the gap between socio-economic 
classes. The COVID-19 pandemic 
saw a rise in digital apps providing 
personalised medical services. This 
created a surge in the availability 
and accessibility of medical help—to 
those who would traditionally have had 
limited access to support. Similarly, the 
medical and pharmaceutical industry 
made significant advancements during 
COVID-19. Should the pace of innovation 
continue, we may see more personalised 
digital healthcare. 
 
Companies devoted to improving the 
future of health and wellbeing include 
Bit.bio. Ranked 6 on the Growth 
Economy Top 50, It is focused on 
developing scalable technologies to 
create new gene therapies and enhance 
drug discovery. Bit.bio has joined the 
United Nations Race to Zero campaign 
committing to contribute to global 
sustainability. Similarly, Mogrify, ranked 
19 aims to combat illnesses such as 
retinal and optic nerve degeneration 
through cell reprogramming.

Transition to a sustainable economy
8
The United Nations defines a sustainable 
economy as one that “meets the needs 
of the present without compromising 
the ability of future generations to meet 
their own needs.” It should offer a good 
quality of life to all people, and enhance 
social inclusion while maintaining 
the healthy functioning of the Earth’s 
ecosystem. 
 
Creating a sustainable world requires 
decoupling of the Earth’s resources, 
a transition from a linear to a circular 
economy, financial support, and a 
commitment to change by governments 
and businesses. Decoupling of natural 
resources refers to reduced use of 
natural resources per unit of economic 
activity. For example, reducing the 
use of fossil energies in business by 
adopting a more renewable energy 
source such as solar power. A circular 
economy consumes less, consumes 
more efficiently, and creates systematic 
change. It focuses on how we can use 
renewable resources effectively to 
protect the Earth’s ecosystem. 
 
Companies leading change in this 
area include, Dropless ranked 4 on the 
Growth Economy Top 50. Dropless is 
a sustainable vehicle care service. Its 
unique selling point is its use of non-
hazardous water solutions. Its method of 
cleaning vehicles reduces water waste 
and toxic spillage in water sources. 
Likewise, Oddbox, ranked 8 aims to 
combat food waste in the UK. Oddbox 
delivers boxes of oddly sized fruit and 
vegetables—that would have otherwise 
been wasted—to businesses and 
consumers. Since its inception in 2015, 
Oddbox says it has saved 34.1t of fruit 
and vegetables, 3.6m litres of water, and 
37.8t of carbon emissions.

Innovation and emerging technologies
9
COVID-19 accelerated the need 
for digitisation in business and our 
daily lives. It impacted our mobility, 
availability, and capacity to interact with 
others. The development and adoption 
of new technologies that bridged 
physical distances provided unique ways 
to work, socialise, and communicate. 
The rise of hybrid working introduced 
a new wave of accessibility as millions 
of individuals could now work from the 
comfort of their homes. Innovative and 
emerging technologies bring a breadth 
of opportunities for businesses. For 
instance, they create employment, 
improve user experiences, and remove 
human error from high risk projects. 
Equally, whilst innovative and emerging 
technologies provide opportunities, they 
also present many complex challenges. 
There is a risk of potential labour 
dislocation, issues concerning legal 
regulation, and collective governance. 
 
Companies leading in innovation 
and emerging technologies include 
Redwood Bank which has claimed the 
top spot in the Growth Economy Top 
50. Redwood Bank provides specialist 
financial advice to small and medium-
sized British enterprises by using 
the latest technologies. Following its 
incorporation in 2016, Redwood Bank 
has raised £39.8m in equity investment. 
Another company bringing an innovative 
approach to a traditional industry is 
Rovco. Ranked at 21, Rovco provides 
underwater surveying services for 
energy companies. It uses artificial 
intelligence and robotics to provide 
detailed, efficient, and high-quality 
services for maritime security, offshore 
renewables, and scientific research. 
Since its incorporation in 2016, 
Rovco has secured £32.9m of equity 
investment.

Geopolitics and demographics
10
The advance of emerging markets China, 
India, and Brazil have expanded the 
economic importance of the countries, 
creating a shift in geopolitics. Similarly, 
the rise of digitisation, the impact of 
global warming, migration, and political 
conflicts have contributed to increasing 
tensions amongst superpowers. 
 
Climate change has had a notable 
influence on geopolitics and shifting 
demographics. Changes to the Earth’s 
ecosystem have led to environmental 
degradation and increased migration. 
Another contentious issue for 
governments is the ageing population. 
The United Nations predicts that the 
ageing population (aged 65+) will soon 
outnumber children below the age of 
five. This places a strain on governments 
and economies to provide efficient 
resources when resources are becoming 
increasingly scarce. Ageing populations 
are most prevalent in western countries. 
Contrastingly in Africa and India, those 
aged 15 and under outnumber the 
ageing population. The Russia-Ukraine 
War is a paradigm of how geopolitical 
conflict affects the international 
community. Russia controls the majority 
of European gas exports and the current 
war has led to sanctions, limited exports, 
increased energy prices and further 
tensions among global powers. 
 
A diverse group of companies are 
working to tackle these issues and 
ameliorate risk.  Element is working to 
ensure that governments, businesses, 
and individuals can communicate 
privately on secure platforms. Element 
is 43 on the Growth Economy Top 50. 
Working to support the development of 
the young population are companies like 
N Family Club. Ranked at 30, the nursery 
chain organises events for parents to 
support their child’s early development. 
For every child they educate at N Family 
Club, they support a nursery-age child 
affected by conflict across the world.

Whilst the US dominates the 
global technology vertical by 
market capitalisation, benefitting 
from unparalleled infrastructure, 
concentrated regions of expertise 
(including Silicon Valley and Austin, 
TX), best-in-class tech-orientated 
universities (MIT, CalTech), and a 
significant, homogenous market 
in which to launch services; the 
UK continues to punch well above 
its weight as a hub for innovation 
and emerging, disruptive software 
solutions. This is particularly 
apparent with software-as-a-
service companies within the 
Singer Growth Economy receiving 
£94.5b in equity investment from 
2012-H1/2022, outperforming any 
other sector. A combination of a 
highly skilled and well-educated 
workforce (benefitting from its 
own world-class education hubs 
such as Cambridge and Oxford), 
governmental support (tax 
incentives, low-touch regulation) 
and investors’ strong conceptual 
understanding of new ideas are 
critical drivers of capital availability 
to a range of innovative young 
companies. For example, with 
regards to the emerging theme 
Industry 4.0, London is second 
only to Silicon Valley in terms of 
the number of related startups it is 
home to (Silicon Valley: 89, London: 
50, NYC: 39). 
 
Whilst we see fewer business-to-
consumer (B2C) ‘category killers’ 
emerging from the UK than the 
US, what is notable is a talent 
for identification and creation of 
solutions targeting specific niche 
business issues (B2B solutions). 
UK technology benefits from 
being able to interact closely 
with large, global businesses and 
source knowledgeable industry 
talent to help support and drive 
innovation. This supports first-
mover advantage, and strong 
positions in technology sub-sectors. 
For example, a rich UK heritage in 
financial services has supported a 
highweighting towards disruptive 
fintech companies within this 
year’s Top 50 rankings (Moneybox, 
Monese, Revolut et al). 
 
Digital transformation remains a 
highly investable theme across 
UK public markets, offering 
continued attractive growth 
in fundamentals despite the 
weakening macroeconomic 
backdrop. UK publicly-listed 
companies with exposure to the 
digitisation and process automation 
theme include value-added 
consultancies like Kin + Carta and 
Next Fifteen; resellers like Bytes, 
Softcat and Computacenter; and 
other notable names such as Blue 
Prism and Thoughtonomy (process 
automation), GlobalData (business 
intelligence) and Sage (business 
cloud). 
 
From the Top 50 rankings, the 
following companies within the 
digital process and automation 
theme catch our eye: 
 
ContractPodAI enables 
the automation of contract 
management for law firms 
and corporations. Automation 
of contract processing has 
applications across a variety of 
enterprise departments and all 
verticals, creating a significant 
market to play into. 
 
Quantexa uses big data analytics 
and machine learning to unlock 
a company’s first-party data 
resources, enabling enterprises to 
identify hidden opportunities and 
risks in order to support customer 
decision-making. 
 
Cutover develops software aimed 
at improving the integration of 
human and machine workflows, by

The financial services world has 
for a long time been dominated 
by large, established financial 
institutions. Following the financial 
crisis, the majority of these 
players were facing numerous 
pressure points which have led 
to higher competition, increased 
commoditisation, and ultimately, 
more and more consolidation. 
Outdated technology infrastructure 
and the limited flexibility often 
inherent in large organisations, 
have resulted in increasingly one-
dimensional products and services. 
This led to limited provision of 
accessible and suitable products 
and services for numerous client 
segments. 
 
The idea of finance for everyone 
has found itself in many mission 
statements of rapidly growing 
finance/fintech companies. Strong 
growth among solutions, such 
as retail investment and trading 
platforms as well as challenger 
banks, underpins the requirement 
for the provision of accessible and 
suitable products and services 
to underserved client segments, 
including the mass affluent/retail 
and the wider SME space. 
 
Additionally, the following 
structural trends have resulted 
in the emergence of niches and 
underserved market segments: 
 
Challenger banks and FX solutions 
Challenger bank platforms, such 
as Monzo, have taken a significant 
space in the market, benefitting 
from the high proportion of 
international professionals in 
the country who maintain a high 
demand for cross-border financial 
services. Whilst large, established 
high-street banks are usually 
more rigid, opaque and relatively 
expensive, we see a number of 
technology-enabled platforms and 
challenger banks, such as Revolut 
and Monese, with a focus on cross-
border FX capabilities for smaller 
clients, more nimble offerings and 
better customer service. 
 
Savings and investment 
The savings gap in the UK and 
the shift of responsibility to plan 
for retirement onto the individual 
mark some of the most significant 
structural drivers in the financial

About this report 
This report analyses the 40.6k private, high-
growth companies that comprise the Singer 
Growth Economy. Companies that met one of 
Beauhurst’s eight triggers (see page 5) and 
that have operations in at least one of the 
Singer Growth Economy Themes (page 3) are 
in scope. 
 
The report also includes a ranking of the 
Top 50 high-growth companies using 
a three-year compound annual growth 
rate (CAGR) for the higher of turnover or 
employee headcount. To be eligible for the 
ranking, companies need to have grown their 
valuation by at least a 15% CAGR between 
01/07/2019 and 30/06/2022 based on at least 
two equity finance deals during the period. 
 
The report has been produced using 
Beauhurst’s data on high-growth and equity-
backed UK companies. 
 
High-growth companies 
Beauhurst identifies private UK companies 
that are high growth or have high-growth 
ambition using eight triggers. If a company 
meets one of the triggers (outlined on page 
5), the company is considered to be high 
growth or have high-growth ambition. For 
more detail on the growth triggers, please
